lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- What Do You Think? Strong Enough, Not Too Strong
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 16 -- What Do You Think?
lesson.grammar_point: hedging language: may, might, could + verb, probably, it seems that

listenings.text: Thank you, that is a very good question, and I want to be careful with my answer. Our results suggest that the drug may reduce nerve pain, but this is a preliminary finding. We had only forty patients, so it is possible that the effect is smaller in a bigger group. It seems that the patients with recent symptoms responded better, but I am not one hundred percent sure yet, because the two groups were not the same size. So my honest answer is this: it probably works for some patients, and it is unlikely to work for everybody. We need a second study before we can make a strong claim. If you are interested, I can share the data with you after the session.

I see your point, and I think your data is really interesting. But I am not sure we can say that the treatment works. In my opinion, the improvement might be related to the placebo effect, because the patients knew they were getting a new drug. It could also be a question of dosage. You used a high dose, and in our clinic, patients generally cannot take that dose for a long time. So I would say the results are promising, but probably not conclusive for now. Maybe the next step is a trial where the patients and the doctors do not know who gets the real drug.

extra_audio.text: Our results suggest that the drug may reduce nerve pain. But this is a preliminary finding, because we had only forty patients. It seems that the patients with recent symptoms responded better. So it probably works for some patients, but it is unlikely to work for everybody. paras: A few years ago, a small study with thirty patients found that a common drug might reduce nerve pain. The authors were careful. They wrote that the result was preliminary and that more research was needed. One week later, a newspaper published a different story: "Old drug cures nerve pain." The study did not change. Only the words changed.

Scientists call this careful language hedging. Words like may, might and could, and phrases like "it seems that" or "our data suggest", show how certain the speaker is. They are not a sign of weakness. A good researcher separates a claim from an assumption, and says clearly when a result is likely, unlikely or still uncertain.

Hedging is also polite. In a Q&A, it is a way to disagree without attacking. "I'm not 100% sure, but I think the effect could be related to the dose" opens a conversation. "You are wrong" closes it. Of course, there is a limit: if every sentence has three maybes, the listener cannot find your message. The goal is not to hide your opinion, but to show exactly how strong it is.

choices: Newspapers report science with the same words that the scientists use in their papers.
Careful words like might and may show how strong a claim is, and help scientists disagree politely.
Scientists should never give an opinion in a Q&A, because they are often wrong about their own data and other people notice it.
